chapter_theme: The first fifteen poems of Kapilar's kurinjikkali: secret love on the hill told as scenes, from the girl's staged fall from the swing (37) and the old playmate who seizes her wrist and is shielded by her lie (51) to the friend's disclosure and the kuravai wedding (39); a run of valli songs sung while pounding grain (40 to 43) alternates reproach of the absent lover with its own refutation until the hidden listener comes to marry; and the friend's speeches to the man measure the girl's wasting by the things of his own hill, refuse his night visits and praise his giving to shame him into marriage.

37.reading: The girl tells her friend about a young man who kept coming with a garland and a bow, like a hunter tracking a beast, looking at her and signing but never speaking of his sickness; sleepless, and afraid he might pass on without her ever seeing, she dared one shameless act: by the millet field where they scare off the parrots she asked him to push her on the swing, let go, and fell as if by accident onto his chest; he caught her up at once, she lay there as if she had fainted, and the moment she stirred and rose he sent her off with 'go, girl of the bright locks', such is his fine decency.
37.nuance: Lines 8 and 9 give the rule she breaks: he cannot speak to her face, and for a woman to speak is unwomanly, so a staged fall does the work of the word. The comedy has two pretences, her fall and her swoon, and line 17 says he took the fall for real (வாய்யாச் செத்து); his sending her away the instant she stirs leaves open whether he saw through her, and it is that restraint she praises.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots, the kurinji meeting place of kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the young man coming again and again with garland and bow, like a hunter tracking a strong beast by its prints

38.reading: The friend tells the girl how she spoke to the hill lord, in whose land a rutting elephant, taking a flowering vengai for a tiger, gores its trunk and, unable to pull its tusk free, bellows through the clefts like the ten-headed demon king straining beneath the god's mountain: when he comes by night through the hard path, heedless of snakes and the dark and the hill, she who had drooped like a field without water, like a poor man's youth, like the old age of one who never kept to virtue, grows lovely at dawn like a field after rain, like the wealth of a gracious man and the gain of a capable one; has he a way to keep that beauty from fading and from slander? and now, having heard her grief told, the good hill lord comes, seeing the vengai in flower, to marry her.
38.nuance: The three stanzas use the moral similes of the didactic books (the poor man's youth, the gracious man's wealth) as a scale for a girl's face, and each ends with a challenge: if he can keep this beauty, let him say how; the only way is marriage, and the close says he has understood. The elephant that wounds the vengai in error and is caught by its own tusk may glance at the hero, and the vengai flowering is the wedding season (line 25), but only one correspondence is drawn, so ullurai is not tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill elephant at the flowering vengai and the hill lord's night visits

comparisons.tenor: the elephant straining to free its tusk from the vengai, like the demon king who could not lift the god's mountain
the flowering vengai, which looks like a tiger
the girl drooping after the night's fear, like a field without water
the girl growing lovely at dawn, like a field that has had rain
the girl's drooping, like the youth of a man with no wealth
her renewed beauty, like the wealth of a man strong in grace
her wasting, like the old age of one who never kept to virtue
her renewed beauty, like the gain of a capable man

39.reading: The friend tells the girl how she told the village that the girl, swept off by a swift flood in which she was bathing, her eyes shut in fear, was saved by a hill chief's son who leapt in, garland swinging, and carried her out held to his chest, so that by that embrace she is one who could bring rain at need; that the hill people keep to the right, so the valli does not fail, the honey is not lost and the millet yields, and because their women rise worshipping their husbands their men's arrows never miss; that the mother told the brothers, who glared a whole day at their bows and arrows, then said neither of the two was at fault and bowed their heads; and she bids the girl dance the kuravai with her lover to please the god of the hill, imagining how at the wedding the two will act as strangers, and how the hill lord has now come with the wise and the elders to end her pallor, the gossip and the stolen meetings.
39.nuance: Lines 5-6 and 17-18 make a claim close to the one the Kural makes of the wife who rises worshipping her husband and commands the rain, but here the power is earned by one embrace before marriage and extended to the hill's whole livelihood (tubers, honey, millet, the hunters' arrows): the friend's disclosure is an argument that the girl has already kept faith. Line 46's chain of rhyming words describes someone who knows the signs and the reckoning, probably the one who fixes the wedding day; the referent is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: disclosure of a hill love to the kin and a wedding before the hill god

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes, called lotus
the moon resting on the hill, which the hill people take for a honeycomb and build a ladder to
the girl's kohl-lined eyes, called neythal petals
the girl's shoulders, like bamboo

40.reading: The friend calls the girl to sing a valli song as they pound the millet heads in a sandal mortar with a pearl-set tusk for pestle, praising the hill of the man who gave her a sickness without enmity: the friend sings it as the hill of one who ends his kin's distress, where kanthal clusters like the joined hands of hill women worshipping the peak drip honey, and of one who would grieve more than those he loves if their old beauty faded, where a soft-fingered she-monkey pleads her want amid an untaught male's crowding band; the girl, turning it against him, sings the hill of one who takes a woman's beauty and leaves her like a bee that drinks pollen on the slope, where nymphs bathe in the cold falls after ball-play; and the last stanza praises the hill of one who says he will never leave his own, where a tusker bends down tall sugarcane for his mate's craving in pregnancy; and the friend says he heard their song, came in full of joy, and made the girl's breasts bloom, the lord of the hill.
40.nuance: The song alternates praise and reproach, each stanza setting a hill-thing beside a claim about the man; the reproach is sung so the man will hear it, and the last stanza's tusker answers the girl's bee: the one leaves the flower, the other bends the cane for his mate. Lines 8 to 28 and 31 to 34 are not in the sangamtamil.com text, so this reading rests on one witness.

thinai_evidence.note: millet pounding, kanthal, the tusker and the hill women of the kurinji slope

comparisons.tenor: the millet heads hanging low, like good women standing in modesty
the kanthal clusters, like the joined hands of hill women worshipping the peak
the girl's body, lovely as tender shoots
the man who takes a woman's beauty and leaves, as a bee leaves a flower

iraicchi.act: the tusker bends down tall sugarcane to feed his mate's craving in pregnancy
iraicchi.sense: the man who says he will not leave his own will care for her as the tusker cares for his mate

41.reading: The friend calls the girl to pound bamboo rice in a rock mortar, a tusk for pestle and a chembu leaf for winnow, and sing of the hill lord in whose land, at a thundering midnight lit by lightning, a hunter hears an elephant feeding with its mate, climbs his platform and slings a stone that scatters vengai flowers, brings down ripe aasini fruit, pierces a honeycomb, tears through mango clusters and a plantain leaf and lodges in a jackfruit; they sing his hill as the hill of one who broke his oath, then deny he could lie, for a falsehood in his truth would be fire in the moon; as the hill of one who has not come though her bangles slip, then deny he could stay away, for that in a kind man would be a kuvalai scorched in a shaded pool; as the hill of one who has left her, then deny he would, for that in a bond would be darkness in the sun; and she ends that it went well: the man, listening hidden, came, and her father, sitting under the wedding vengai, consented to the match.
41.nuance: The stone's flight (lines 10 to 16) runs through five trees and a honeycomb in one sentence before it comes to rest, one throw disturbing the whole hill; nothing in the poem matches it to the lovers, so it is scene. Each refrain states the reproach and then takes it back with an impossible image, so the girls accuse and acquit him in the same breath for the hidden listener.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter's platform, vengai and aasini of the hill

comparisons.tenor: a falsehood appearing in the truthful hill lord
unkindness appearing in one who is kind
desertion appearing in a bond of love
his hill shining like an uncut gem

42.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the good hill, where a fan-eared elephant that ended its old feud with a tiger eats leaves and sleeps to the roar of the white falls, has forgotten them, so let him forget, they know well what he was to them; let them pound bamboo rice with a killer elephant's tusk and sing: his hill's falls gleam like swords, yet he is shameless; would a man of straight, unbending, right-loving heart abandon those who long for him? the kongu flowers make his hill look like elephants decked in gold, yet he is a waster; would one gentler than his hill's water, who gives chariots to those who seek him, leave her to pining? the honeycomb on his peak shows like the moon slipping into cloud, yet he has hurt her; then she stops herself: do not speak of his cruelty, he is no lawless man who fears nothing that should be feared; he heard them from hiding, drew the girl by the hand to his chest, and her pallor vanished like darkness before the sun.
42.nuance: The defence is in the vocabulary of kingship and law (நேர்கோல், அறம் புரி நெஞ்சத்தவன், அறன் இலி), so the girls acquit the lover by the standard of a just ruler; line 26 recalls the maxim that the wise fear what ought to be feared. Lines 11 to 22 and 25 to 32 are not in the sangamtamil.com text, and line 31 recurs in poem 145.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's elephant, kongu blossom and falls

comparisons.tenor: the falls of his hill, sword-bright
the hills covered in kongu blossom, like elephants decked in gold
the honeycomb on the peak, like the moon entering a cloud
the girl's pallor vanishing at his embrace, like darkness before the sun

43.reading: The friend calls the girl to pound white hill paddy in a rock mortar with a pestle of the tusk of an elephant that killed a tiger and of sandalwood, and to sing the man of the rich hill as one praises a lord: she sings his hill, where a dragonfly sits on kanthal buds like rings on the fingers of noble women, as the hill of one who will not give way to an enemy though death come and is not ashamed to lose to his friends; the girl sings it, where bamboo sheaths fall like the ears of a spotted deer, as the hill of one who never speaks of others' faults though they wrong him; and again, where plantain bunches hang like a tiger's paw, as the hill of one who, if he could not fill the want of one who told him of poverty, would give up his own body; and as they sang his worth together the girl's wasted shoulders swelled, as if he had come and been gracious.
43.nuance: The three virtues sung are puram virtues (steadfastness in enmity, restraint of speech, giving to the point of death), so the akam lover is praised as a hero; the cure is worked by the praise itself before he comes (போன்றே, as if). The hill-things and the virtues are only set side by side, with no part matched to part, so neither ullurai nor iraicchi is tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: hill paddy, kanthal and the mountain goat of the kurinji slope

comparisons.tenor: singing the hill lord, as one praises a chief
the dragonfly sitting on the kanthal bud, like a ring on a noble woman's finger
the bamboo sheath falling away, like the ear of a spotted deer
the elephant moving like a hill
the curved plantain bunches, like a tiger's paw
the girl's shoulders swelling at the song, as if he had come and been gracious

44.reading: The friend tells the lord of the fragrant hill, where a loud waterfall shakes an old vengai so that its ripe flowers fall on a handsome elephant and then on a lotus, which glows as if the goddess of fortune sat there in delight, that though her own grief grew the girl hid his ungraciousness even from the friend, ashamed that the friend would blame him before others; hid it from the street, ashamed they would say he does not keep his word; hid it from her companions, ashamed they would speak of his false want of character; and since, with a nature rare even in a mother, she guarded him from blame, let them hurry to her, lord, as the medicine for her grief.
44.nuance: The friend tells the man the fault the girl hid by praising her for hiding it, so the praise is the reproach, and he learns of it from the very person it was hidden from. The opening lotus under falling vengai flowers is the image of fortune at rest, set against a girl who has none.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, elephant and falls of the hill slope

comparisons.tenor: the lotus strewn with vengai flowers, glowing as if the goddess of fortune sat on it in delight
the man's coming to the girl, the medicine for her grief

45.reading: The friend tells the girl how she asked the lord of the high hill, where at dawn the hot sun lights a kanthal cluster by a spring, thunder in a mountain-shaking storm strikes it, taking it for a jewel-hooded snake drinking, and the small village wakes to the echo, whether he ruined the girl's flower eyes to pallor because they resembled the flowers of his hill's springs, wasted her shoulders because they resembled the bamboo of his slopes where tusker and tiger fight, withered her beauty because it resembled the blazing vengai of his clefts; and that since she reproached him with his many faults and their secret meetings grew rare, he has fixed their wedding for a day that pleases him.
45.nuance: The three questions run the stock comparisons of beauty backwards: the likeness of her eyes, shoulders and beauty to the things of his hill becomes the mock reason he destroyed them, as if he treated her as part of his land. The thunder that strikes a flower mistaken for a snake is another scene of harm by mistaken identity, as in poems 38 and 49, but no pairs are anchored, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: kanthal, bamboo and vengai of the hill, set as likenesses of the girl

comparisons.tenor: the kanthal cluster by the spring, which the thunder takes for a jewel-hooded snake drinking
the storm wind and rain, as if overturning a great mountain
the girl's eyes, which resemble the flowers of his hill's springs
the girl's shoulders, which resemble the bamboo of his slopes
the girl's beauty, which resembles the flaming vengai clusters
the girl's forehead, like the crescent moon

46.reading: The friend tells the lord of the fine hill, where a dark-winged bee that left its flowers to hunt flits between a tusker and a tiger in fight, settling on the tiger as on a vengai bough and on the elephant's spotted face, like envoys who make friends of angry kings, that the girl hears he complains: that on a thundering night he got no chance and turned back, while she, longing to meet, lay pining at the trysting place with her ears strained to the nochchi; that he crossed the hard way and found no grace, while she, under a vow to the high god, pined with many cares; that on a stormy midnight he found no signal because she slept, and will blame her to her friend, while she longed for his grace like the bird that sings up to the sky for raindrops; and the friend says that if he too turns angry with her, sleepless in her sickness, he wins only by falsehood, for her bright bangles, like the echo of his hill, tell all of her sickness.
46.nuance: The speaker shifts: lines 10 to 21 are in the girl's first person and address a woman (புனை இழாய்), while lines 1 to 9 and 23 to 27 address the man and speak of the girl as இவள்; the reading takes the friend as voicing the girl's words, which is not certain. The bee that blunders between two fighters like a peacemaking envoy is close to the friend's own position between quarrelling lovers, but the marker joins it to envoys, not to the lovers, so ullurai condition 2 fails; a near miss.

thinai_evidence.note: a kurinji night tryst at the nochchi, with tiger and tusker on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the bee flitting between the fighting tusker and tiger, like envoys who make friends of angry kings
the striped tiger, which the bee takes for a vengai bough
the girl longing for his grace, like the bird singing up for raindrops
the girl's bangles telling her sickness, like the echo of his hill

47.reading: The girl tells her friend of a man who speaks humbly like one begging yet has the strength of one who could guard the world, the restraint of one who has learned from the wise, and the power of one who can ease the poor by giving: such a man, putting off his manliness, tells her that he cannot live without her, that she does not know how he suffers, that he will not live if she leaves him; yet his words are hard to believe, a woman can hardly decide alone, and to be called the one who gave way is a reproach; they must think it out together; she will make as if to say 'come, only for an embrace', and she tells her heart not to go the way he wants.
47.nuance: The four portraits at the start are all built with போல், so his virtues are given as appearances, which suits a speaker deciding whether to trust him. Lines 9 to 17 set three of his sayings against three reasons for doubt in a run of conditionals (ஆயின்), and the poem ends not with a decision but with a feint: she will seem to consent and keep her heart back.

thinai_evidence.note: a man's pleading in secret love, the occasion of kurinji union

comparisons.tenor: the man's humble speech, like one begging a favour
the man's strength, like one who could guard the world
the man's restraint, like one who learned from the wise
the man's power, like one able to ease the poor by giving

48.reading: The friend tells the lord of the hill, where a great tiger, its neck swollen with strength, is confused among a herd of tuskers whose spotted, bee-hummed, ichor-wet faces look like flowering vengai, asking whether the girl's shoulders are at fault that, listening for him through the rainy nights, her bangles slip before her watchful mother like the ripe kodal flowers of his slope; whether her eyes are at fault that, sleepless in the dark and longing for him, they weep before the clamouring neighbours like the rain-beaten blue lily of his spring; whether her skin, like a gem tried on gold, is at fault that its pallor tells her wasting like the trembling shoots of his grove; she fears even to soothe the girl to sleep with the hope that he will return the love he left, for the grief she bears, weighed, is greater than the hill whose bounds no one knows.
48.nuance: Each question clears a part of the girl (shoulders, eyes, skin) of a fault and so lays it on him, and each likens the sign of her grief to a thing of his own land, as if his country testified against him. Lines 21 and 22 are hard to construe: the reading takes பின் ஈதல் வேண்டும் ... நட்பு as the hope the friend fears to offer, which is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: kodal, blue lily and vengai of the hill, likened to the girl's wasting

comparisons.tenor: the spotted faces of the tuskers, like flowering vengai
the girl's bangles slipping, like ripe kodal flowers falling
the girl's eyes shedding tears, like the rain-beaten blue lily
the girl's dark skin, like a gem tried on gold
the girl's wasting, like the trembling shoots of his grove

49.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where an elephant sleeping on the slope, weary from beating off a tiger, sees the fight again in a dream, starts up in fright, takes a newly flowered vengai for the tiger and wrecks its beauty, then, its rage spent, cannot bear to look at the tree and bows its head in shame, that his love for the girl is sweet but his coming is bitter: through a hard path in lightning, thunder and rain; through cloud-wrapped slopes haunted by spirits; spear in hand, not counting that he is alone, through paths where elephants roam; so let him not come by night, and by day he will have her broad soft shoulders, on the slope where mingled flowers stripe the wide rock.
49.nuance: The elephant that wrecks the vengai in error and then cannot look at it may glance at the lover, whose night visits endanger the girl he loves; but only one correspondence is drawn (harm in error, then shame), so by condition 3 it is scene, a near miss for ullurai. The refrain separates the man's love, which is sweet, from his coming, which is bitter, so that refusing the night tryst does not refuse him.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger, elephant and vengai of the night path on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes, called opening flowers
the girl's dark hair, like darkness

50.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shining hill streams, where a great she-elephant that has eaten bamboo and curved paddy stalks enters a plantain thicket and a young mountain goat sleeps where she passed, that since, with his hand resting on his strong bow, he looked at her friend until she forgot to drive the parrots from the millet, he must not now put it off long: the girl is the dear daughter of poor folk in a small village that eats jackfruit ripened on the rock, while he surpasses the rain in giving wind-swift chariots and elephants to the poets who come; and though she knows he has no cruelty, like a whip that only touches a swift horse, she urges him: her friend's beauty, cherished as people rear a mountain goat's kid, leaves her when he leaves her side.
50.nuance: Lines 12 to 17 set the girl's poor family against the man's wealth and his fame for giving to poets; the friend praises the patron's giving to shame him into giving the girl her due, so a puram virtue is turned into an akam obligation. The whip simile excuses the urging itself: even a good horse is touched.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarded from parrots and the mountain goat of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the friend's urging of a man who has no cruelty, like the whip that only touches a swift horse
the care with which the girl's beauty has been cherished, like people rearing a mountain goat's kid

51.reading: The girl tells her friend of the naughty boy who used to kick down the sand houses they built in the street, pull the garlands from their hair and run off with their striped ball: one day, while she and her mother sat at home, he came asking for drinking water; her mother told her to pour it from the golden vessel and give it to him; she went, not knowing who it was, and he seized her bangled wrist and squeezed it; in panic she cried 'mother, see what this one did', and as her mother came running she said 'he choked on the water', and her mother stroked his back, while he, looking at her from the corner of his eye as if to kill her, smiled at her, that thief's son.
51.nuance: The turn is her quick lie: having cried out, she covers for him, and the mother's stroking of his back makes the mother an unknowing party to the secret; his side-glance and smile seal a complicity the girl has chosen. கள்வன் மகன் is affectionate abuse: the thief is the one who has stolen her heart, and the old playmate who broke their sand houses has returned as a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the first bold touch of secret love, kept secret by the girl's own lie

comparisons.tenor: the young man's side-glance at her, as if to kill

links.note: Kural 1257: the woman says she knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she longs for. Kalittokai 37: the girl says that, since he could not speak and she might not, she resolved (துணிதந்து) to do one shameless deed (நாண் இன்மை செய்தேன்), staging a fall into his arms.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the loss of shame something that happens to a woman when the lover acts, while Kapilar's girl chooses the shameless act herself because the man will not, and then praises him for the restraint that sends her home; held together they show that akam allows the heroine to set aside naanam as a tactic when the rules of speech leave both lovers mute.

links.note: Both use the simile of a poor man's youth (பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை, 38 line 15; the waste's trees in 10): poem 10 measures a withered landscape by it, poem 38 the girl's face drooping after a night of fear.
links.teaches: The paalai poet and Kapilar draw on one stock of moral similes, but Kapilar moves it from the land to the woman's body and pairs it with its opposite (the gracious man's wealth), so the girl's face becomes a landscape that his coming can drought or rain on, which is the kali form's way of turning a moral maxim into a lover's argument for marriage.

links.note: Kural 55: the wife who rises worshipping her husband, not a god, commands rain. Kalittokai 39: the girl, embraced by the man who saved her from the flood, could bring rain at need (line 6), and because hill women rise worshipping their husbands (கேள்வர்த் தொழுது எழலால்) the hunters' arrows do not miss.
links.teaches: The Kural's claim appears in the friend's disclosure as a belief the hill folk already hold, extended from rain to the whole hill economy and staked on a single premarital embrace, so the maxim on the wife's power was a shared folk conviction that the friend could use to argue the girl was already a faithful wife.

links.note: Kural 957: a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon. Kalittokai 41: if a falsehood appeared in the hill lord's truth it would be like fire appearing in the moon (திங்களுள் தீத் தோன்றியற்று).
links.teaches: The Kural uses the moon to say a noble man's fault cannot be hidden; the girls use it to say such a fault is impossible, so the same figure that warns the great serves in akam as a pledge of trust sung for the lover to overhear, binding him to live up to it.

links.note: Kural 428: not to fear what should be feared is folly, and to fear it is the work of the wise. Kalittokai 42 line 26: the friend checks her own reproach, saying he is not a lawless man who fears nothing that should be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சா அறன் இலி அல்லன்).
links.teaches: The Kural's prudence about danger is turned by the friend into a moral standard for a lover, where what should be feared is breaking a girl's heart, and failing it makes a man அறன் இலி; the pair shows the maxim already working as a test of character in love, not only in counsel.

links.note: Kural 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach. Kalittokai 43 lines 26-27: the lover is praised as one who, if he could not fill the want of one who told him of poverty, would give up his body (தன் மெய் துறப்பான்).
links.teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is sung by the girls as a fact about one man to cure a girl's wasting, so the ethical maxim served in akam as the highest praise a lover could receive, and the praise itself works the cure before he comes.

links.note: Kural 980: greatness hides another's weakness, smallness tells only faults. Kalittokai 44: the girl hid the man's ungraciousness from her friend, the street and her companions, ashamed that others would blame him, and the friend calls this a nature rare even in a mother.
links.teaches: The Kural's mark of greatness is shown in the one wronged, a girl hiding her lover's fault, and the friend's report of it becomes a reproach, since the man learns that the greater one in the affair is she; the pair shows the maxim working as leverage in a love quarrel.

links.note: Kural 1112: the man scolds his heart for reeling at flowers, thinking her eyes resemble what many can see. Kalittokai 45: the friend asks whether he ruined the girl's eyes because they resembled the flowers of his hill's springs (மலர் ஏய்க்கும்). On one reading the claims are incompatible: the Kural's lover refuses the likeness as beneath her, Kalittokai's friend holds him to it as the motive of harm.
links.teaches: The flower comparison that the Kural's lover rejects to honour the girl is used by the friend against the man as an accusation, so the same convention of beauty can be denied as praise or pressed as a charge, depending on whether the lover or the friend wields it.

links.note: Kural 1192: the grace a lover shows the one who loves is like rain to those who live by it. Kalittokai 46: the girl longed for his grace like the bird that sings up to the sky for raindrops (துளி நசை ... அளி நசை), yet it was a stormy midnight (கனை பெயல் நடுநாள்) that kept him from the tryst.
links.teaches: The Kural's image of grace as rain is set in Kalittokai against real rain, which is what stopped the meeting, so the girl craves one rain while the other keeps it from her; the pairing shows the kali poet testing a stock equivalence against the weather of the kurinji night.

links.note: Kural 1133: the man says he once had shame and sound manliness and now has the palmyra horse. Kalittokai 47: the girl says a man of great strength and restraint has put off his manliness (தன் ஆண்தகை விட்டு) to tell her he cannot live without her.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the lover's own account of losing his manliness, the threat behind the madal, while Kalittokai gives the girl's hearing of it, weighing whether to believe it and what consenting would cost her name, so the pair shows both sides of the same pressure in secret love.

links.note: Kuruntokai 3: the girl says her bond with the hill lord is larger than the earth, higher than the sky, deeper than the sea. Kalittokai 48: the friend tells the hill lord that the girl's grief, weighed, is greater than the hill whose bounds none knows (மலையினும் பெரிதே).
links.teaches: The same kurinji measure by immensity that the girl uses for her love the friend uses for its cost, so the pair shows that the size of the bond and the size of the grief at his absence are one quantity, and the friend can turn the heroine's boast into a charge against the man.

links.note: Both are the friend telling the hill lord not to come by night but by day (இரவின் வாரல் ... பகலும் பெறுவை; இரவின் வருதல் எவனோ? பகல்வரின்), and both open on a tusker after a fight with a tiger, wounded in Akananuru 308, dreaming and ashamed in Kalittokai 49.
links.teaches: Akananuru 308 turns the refusal into a full plan of the day tryst, while Kalittokai 49 builds a triple refrain that calls his love sweet and his coming bitter, so the pair shows the same convention used once as an invitation and once to separate the lover from his risk, with the tiger-fight's aftermath serving each as the danger of the night path.

links.note: Kural 1095: the man says she does not look at him directly but smiles with one eye narrowed. Kalittokai 51: the girl says the young man looked at her from the corner of his eye as if to kill and smiled (கடைக் கண்ணால் ... நகை கூட்டம் செய்தான்).
links.teaches: The Kural reads the sidelong smile as the girl's sign of consent, seen by the man; Kalittokai gives the same sign to the man, seen by the girl after she has lied for him, so the gesture of kurippu is not tied to one sex and seals a secret both have now chosen.

source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai for any poem, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
